full_judgment:
9. Mr. A.Y. Ahmed Ali Sarder, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division erroneously concurred with the findings of the appellate Court that the plaintiff could prove his title to and possession of the suit land without at all the finding arrived at by the trial Court as regards title of the plaintiff and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He further submits that the appellants could prove that in fact, the suit land along with other lands was sold in auction and that their predecessors-in-interest, namely, Entaz Ali, Abdul Hakim and others took settlement of 5.79 acres of land of the suit khatian on payment of salami and that all the Courts below erroneously came to the finding that the defendants could not prove the alleged auction and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. The learned Advocate also submits that the plaintiff created a forged deed of gift dated 28.07.1985 and that the said deed was registered in a different Sub-Registry office by incorporating .01 acre of fictitious land in order to attract jurisdiction of that Sub-Registry office and as such, the deed of gift is void. 

 13. Admittedly, the suit land belonged to Gangadhar Namadas, Nedu Namadas and Nagarbashi Namadas and accordingly, the C.S. Khatian was correctly prepared and published in their names. According to the plaintiff, C.S. recorded tenant, Nagarbashi Namadas died unmarried and as such, his share was inherited by his two full brothers. Gangadhar Namadas sold .35 acre of land out of his share to Shahed Ali and Raj Ali, the predecessors-in-interest of defendant Nos. 2-6, and died leaving behind only daughter Rajeshwari Namadas. The transfer of Gangadhar Namadas to the predecessors-in-interest of defendant Nos. 2-6 was proved by production of relevant volume from the office of the Sub-Registrar, Tangail by PW. 6. The plaintiffs claimed that defendant No. 33 Rajeshwari had no male child and that in the absence of her husband her share was inherited by her uncle's four sons, namely, Khushi Mohan (the plaintiff), Shamvu Charan Mondal, Makhon Mondal and Nani Gopal Mondal. The plaintiffs also claimed that C.S. recorded tenant Nedu Namadas die leaving behind four sons including the plaintiff. The plaintiff asserted that by amicable partition amongst me brothers, he got 3.04 acres of land out of the suit land. The plaintiffs claimed that his brothers transferred their interest in the suit land to him by a registered deed of gift dated 28.03.1985. The plaintiffs produced the original deed of gift (exhibit-2). Having considered the evidence on record, the appellate Court came to a finding that the plaintiff could prove his title to, and possession in the suit land. 

 14. On the other hand, the defendant claimed that the suit land along with other lands was sold in auction. In order to prove the certificate sale, the defendants could not produce the sale certificate and writ of delivery of possession. The trial Court found the defendants could not produce certificate copies of the shelf-index and the sale certificate and in the absence of those important documents, it could be not said that the suit land was sold in auction and as a result, the right, title and interest of C.S. recorded tenants were not extinguished in the suit land. The defendants further claimed that their predecessors-in-interest, Entaz Ali, Abdul Hakim and others obtained lease of 5.79 acres of land of the suit khatian. In order to prove the settlement, the defendants produced exhibit-F/14. The trial Court found that those receipts showing payment of salami did not prove that Entaz Ali, Abdul Hakim, Momtaz Ali Abdul Quddus and Abdul Hye got settlement and possession in the suit land. The trial Court, the appellate Court and the High Court Division concurrently found that the defendants could not prove the alleged auction in support of their claim to suit land.
